# Khaṇḍajātaka (Ja 203)

**ID:** Ja 203
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Khaṇḍajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Love For the Families of Snakes

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Khaṇḍajātaka* (Ja 203), also known as the *Khandhavatta-jātaka*, is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Schober 1997; Schmithausen; Skilling]. According to its traditional frame narrative set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the tale after a monk dies of a snakebite [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010; Schmithausen]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta advises his fellow ascetics to radiate loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward snakes and their royal lineages to protect themselves from harm [Appleton 2010; Schmithausen]. The protective verses recited by the Bodhisatta constitute an early Buddhist snake charm that includes a formula of homage to the Seven Buddhas, an element noted by scholars as reflecting archaic layers of the biographical and *rakṣā* traditions, possibly predating texts such as the *Buddhavamsa* [Holz; Schober 1997].

The verses of Ja 203 are functionally central to the protective chant known as the *Khandhaparitta* (or *Khandha-paritta*) [Holz; Appleton 2010; Skilling]. Direct canonical parallels in Pali include the *Ahirājasutta* (AN 4.67) in the Aṅguttara Nikāya and the *Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka* (Kd 15 / Vin II 109–110) of the Vinaya Cullavagga [SuttaCentral; Schmithausen; Skilling]. Text-reuse computations strongly corroborate these relationships, showing near-verbatim alignment across segments 1.1–6.4 of Ja 203 with Kd 15 and AN 4.67, as well as extensive reuse in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Beyond Pali, related protective verses and narratives against snakebite appear across Buddhist traditions, including the Sanskrit *Upasenasūtra*, the *Mahāmāyūrī*, the *Mahāmantrānusāriṇī*, the *Bower Manuscript*, and Vinaya texts preserved in Tibetan and Chinese translations, such as the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* and the *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [Holz; Schmithausen; DharmaNexus].
